submissions.findingTextShort: A 2026 meta-analysis found improved flow-mediated dilation but no significant blood-pressure, executive-function, or mood benefit in healthy participants.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 randomized controlled trials involving 632 healthy participants found that blueberry interventions improved flow-mediated dilation by 1.11 percentage points (95% CI 0.50 to 1.72; I²=23%), while systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, executive function, and mood showed no statistically significant benefit. The vascular signal should therefore be preserved alongside the null cardiovascular and cognitive outcomes rather than summarized as broad systemic benefit.
submissions.populationContext: Healthy participants across 14 randomized controlled trials; 632 participants total.
submissions.usageContext: Blueberry interventions varied by dose, type, intervention duration, and participant age; this is not evidence that every whole-fruit, powder, or extract preparation has equivalent effects.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Preparation, dose, duration, and age heterogeneity limit generalizability. The null BP, executive-function, and mood outcomes are first-class findings and must not be dropped when presenting the FMD signal. The source must complete registry and semantic-attestation governance before promotion.

submissions.findingTextShort: A 24-week randomized trial found no blueberry effect on p-tau181, neurofilament light, cognitive tests, or systolic blood pressure in cognitively healthy older adults.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A 2026 randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial assigned 57 cognitively healthy older adults to 20 g/day freeze-dried blueberry powder or placebo for 24 weeks. The intervention produced no statistically significant effect on serum p-tau181, neurofilament light, cognitive-test performance, systolic blood pressure, or the other measured brain biomarkers; a secondary analysis found a reduction in diastolic blood pressure.
submissions.populationContext: Fifty-seven cognitively healthy older adults, mean age about 73 years, randomized for 24 weeks.
submissions.usageContext: 20 g/day freeze-dried blueberry powder; the trial does not establish effects for fresh berries, concentrated extracts, or other doses and preparations.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: The modest sample limits precision, and the diastolic-BP result was a secondary outcome. The primary biomarker and cognitive null results should not be obscured by the secondary cardiovascular signal. The source must complete registry and semantic-attestation governance before promotion.

submissions.findingTextShort: A 2025 cognition meta-analysis found episodic- and language-memory signals in older adults with cognitive decline but null results across several other cognitive domains.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of nine randomized trials involving 513 older adults with mild cognitive impairment or subjective cognitive decline found improved episodic memory (SMD 0.34, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.57) and improved language memory in participants with mild cognitive impairment (SMD 0.30, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.60). Processing speed, recognition memory, visuospatial learning, and working memory did not significantly improve.
submissions.populationContext: Older adults with mild cognitive impairment or subjective cognitive decline across nine randomized controlled trials; 513 participants total.
submissions.usageContext: Chronic blueberry intake in cognitively vulnerable older populations; the findings do not establish prevention or treatment of Alzheimer disease or dementia and should not be generalized to healthy younger adults.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Benefits were domain-specific rather than global, and the authors called for further multicenter trials to confirm generalizability and long-term impact. Null cognitive domains must remain visible alongside episodic/language-memory signals. The source must complete registry and semantic-attestation governance before promotion.

submissions.findingTextShort: A metabolic-syndrome meta-analysis found lipid and diastolic-pressure signals but no significant glycemic or anthropometric benefit from blueberry interventions.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A 2021 systematic review included 18 randomized controlled trials and meta-analyzed 12 trials comparing blueberry interventions with placebo. Blueberry interventions significantly reduced total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, and diastolic blood pressure, while glycemic-status markers and anthropometric measurements did not significantly differ from control. Trials varied in blueberry form, dose, participant population, and duration.
submissions.populationContext: Human randomized trials assessing metabolic-syndrome risk factors; populations and baseline metabolic status varied across studies.
submissions.usageContext: Interventions included blueberry powder, extract, fruit, juice, and frozen products; pooled findings must not be presented as preparation-equivalent effects.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Substantial intervention and population heterogeneity limits one-size-fits-all conclusions. Positive lipid/DBP findings and null glycemic/anthropometric outcomes should be preserved together. The source must complete registry and semantic-attestation governance before promotion.
